rv.q: Saunders earns every ‘absolutely fabulous’ accolade the part won her.
Richard Eyre’s production of this Coward classic is beautifully designed.
The best moments come when Saunders is centre-stage, [though] the rest of the cast do ... hold their own.
But under Eyre’s direction, Coward’s 1941 play proves resistant to resuscitation.
These deft little touches are brilliantly orchestrated by Saunders whose stage experience enables her to create an instant rapport with the audience.
Saunders is terrific and the play remains, in the nicest possible way, absolutely fatuous.
So, unlike Elvira’s return to the mortal plane, this play’s revival is, on balance, a good thing for everyone involved.
Yet it seemed like Eyre didn’t have much in the way of ideas for this production other than to make it seem rather old-fashioned, which Coward never really was.
This production, a fine nod to its original, bookended by some splendid individual performances, makes for a delightfully funny night out.
Noël Coward’s play is sprinkled with delightful witticisms but the real scene stealer on this occasion is Jennifer Saunders’s physical comedy.
Yet after establishing the power of popularism, the play becomes unsure of where to go narratively after making its point.
But that’s precisely what it is.

cn.t: Jennifer Saunders shines as Madame Arcati in this polished revival of Coward's supernatural farce, though critics are divided on whether the 80-year-old comedy still feels fresh or merely relies on star power over substance.
